Cities: Skylines Mods & Assets: The Core of the Gameplay

You’re playing Cities: Skylines, building a fictional city you had been working on for weeks, pouring in hours of work every day, just to get the details right.

Suddenly, Paradox Games decided that the game needs an update. Not anything new or fancy — just a small patch.

To the average player it’s not that big a deal. But to you, and hundreds and thousands of players relying on an entire ecosystem of mods supporting their game saves, this is a catastrophic disaster.

Overnight, your save won’t open. Errors pop up like you’ve been hacked. Buildings disappear, or their texture completely turns blue. Older mods break due to incompatibility and corrupt your entire game save.

It’s not the asset creators’ fault. They can’t always predict when developers add patches, and they need time to make mods compatible.

The only thing you could do is try to fix it yourself — scrolling through countless “how to fix broken mods in Cities: Skylines” tutorials on YouTube, or downloading a specific mod that shows you which mods have completely broken and clash with others. Even if you follow every instruction exactly, you might not be able to save your game from eternal destruction after all.

But this shouldn’t be how a mod-dependent gamer plays their game. No one should have to spend hours debugging their saves.

Cities: Skylines was launched in 2015, with new DLCs announced every now and then. The vanilla game gives a cartoonish vibe, filled with vibrant colours and exaggerating facades. Within months, the Steam Workshop brought this game to an entirely new level — a near-professional urban planning software, a stage for thousands of serious players using the base game as the canvas and the mods as paint.

Sure, you could play without mods. For some, this game is aimed at maximising efficiency through traffic design, public transport, and raising taxes to an extent where your residents complain but don’t protest. However, if you were looking to build a beautiful-looking city, it will probably end up looking like a slum, like this:

Vanilla gameplay — cartoonish assets, UI icons everywhere, no mods.

But when you bought the game, you were kinda expecting this:

A modded city — near-photorealistic, built entirely with community assets.

This shows how vital these mods and assets are to this game, as they become a huge — if not the most important — part of the gameplay. These mods turn this game from a relaxing city-building simulator into software for producing highly detailed, miniature real-life cities.

Mods & Assets

The asset and mod creators often produce high quality products that surpass the original game’s models and details, completely for free.

Monaco: Hotel de Paris Monté Carlo — a community-made asset. Free on the Steam Workshop.

The vanilla game only allows you to select an area of land and choose its use — residential, commercial, industrial, and so on. But once you download mods such as Move It and Ploppable RICO, you can actually start planning according to your own vision, instead of having randomly generated buildings placed by the game.

Ploppable RICO Revisited — 6,275 ratings, 85 updates. This mod alone transformed how players build.

To show you the effects of mods, here are screenshots of one of my saves from a few months ago — before it broke down after an update.

(It’s not perfect — it was still under construction. But it gives a glimpse of what you could achieve with mods. Every building you can see is content from individual asset creators, not from Paradox Games.)

The Sequel

Cities: Skylines is now an 11-year-old game, and its sequel, Cities Skylines 2, launched in 2023. In my opinion, the sequel has not reached the height of its predecessor. Paradox Games launched it without mod support, and charged for content — like European building packs — when the community had been making equivalent assets for free for years.

CS2 Creator Packs — paid DLC for content the CS1 community had provided free for a decade.

Players erupted in outrage, and Paradox Games were forced to announce their own content workshop. However, it lacked in variety and volume — it looked like a corner store rather than the supermarket the Steam Workshop had become.

Another issue with the sequel is that it requires so much computing power that the average laptop or PC can’t handle it. CS2 often requires 32GB of RAM or more when building large cities — and some recommend 64GB if you’re playing with mods.

Steam Community, Sept 2023 — “32GB for vanilla. 64GB if you want mods.” This limits who can even play the modded version.

This makes CS2 accessible to fewer people, and limited in mod choice. That is why many players still choose CS1 over the newer game.

Cities: Skylines 1 — Steam Workshop

Look on the left sidebar: 54,978 buildings. 23,026 props. 23,841 vehicles. Built entirely by the community.

Cities: Skylines 2 — Paradox Mods Workshop

The CS2 equivalent — notice how much less content exists compared to CS1’s decade-old ecosystem.

The Need for Change

Once a community has become the author, the developer’s role changes

BeamNG sets an example of how this system should work. By making modding a core pillar of the ecosystem, developers build the game with room for additional community features in mind, making the game structure modular — allowing modders to alter the base game at a fundamental level.

In addition, by collaborating with Automation — a car-building sandbox game — it allows for a complete process of building, tuning, and testing your car, opening the experience to non-modders as well.

This is what I want to see in city-building games and other simulation sandboxes: a game where the player not only builds within a framework, but constructs the framework itself — making their own rules, deciding what content to include, and game developers acknowledging it by updating carefully, with mods in consideration.

Mods in certain games shouldn’t be treated as a fun little addition — an alternative, indie thing on the side. They should be a core feature, allowing individual creators to shine. Not just the developers.
